priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: Proof for the Steel Bin
case.hook: Dr. Priya Nair here. The pond is clean, and the haul is at the recycling center! But Dana won’t fill the steel bin until we prove which things are magnetic steel. Listen to her voicemail below.
case.question: Which haul items go in the steel bin, and what proof should we send Dana?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: A fair test keeps the magnet, the distance and the wait the same. Kai and Mo changed three things, so their results disagreed.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the how-sure dial
clues.t: Names can fool you. A “tin” can is really steel, and it stuck. Test it; don’t guess.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: messy notes to a data table
clues.t: The data table proved it: the steel fork stuck, but the stainless steel spoon did not.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: the fair test
clues.t: In the fair test, only iron and steel things jumped to the magnet. No jump means not magnetic.

solve.title: What goes in the steel bin?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Everything with “steel” or “tin” in its name: the caps, the bean can, the wrench, the fork and the stainless spoon. Send a photo of the bin.
options.why: Check Clue 3. The stainless steel spoon didn’t stick. And a photo isn’t a fair test or a data table.

options.t: Only the shiny things: the caps, the soda can, the spoon and the tag. Shiny is proof enough.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Looks and names can fool you. The soda can and the tag are aluminum.

options.t: The caps, the bean can, the wrench and the fork, because they stuck in a fair test. Send the data table as proof.
options.why: Case cracked! Four items passed the fair test, and the data table is the proof Dana asked for.

options.t: Whatever Kai remembers sticking. No need to write anything down.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Kai and Mo remembered opposite results for the same bottle cap.

bulletin.title: Dana from the recycling center
todo: Press Play and listen. You can read along.
Tap the 3 things Dana needs from us.
lines: Hi, this is Dana at the Palmetto Springs Recycling Center. Thanks for the cleanup haul!
But I can’t put anything in the steel bin [[x:That’s why she called. Now listen for what she NEEDS from you.|just because it looks like steel]].
Please [[fair|run a fair test: the same magnet and the same distance, every time]].
[[table|Write every result in a data table]].
Then [[proof|send me the table as your proof]], and I’ll fill the bin. Bye!
bulletin.win: A fair test, a data table, and the proof. Now find out which items pass!

todo: Read Kai’s page and Mo’s page.

spotdiff.q: Kai and Mo got opposite results. Whose result should Ranger Bell trust?

opts.t: Neither yet. Test again with the same magnet, the same distance and the same wait.

opts.miss: Maybe! But Kai and Mo changed three things. Until the test is fair, you can’t be sure.
8 cm is far, and a weak magnet might not reach. That test isn’t fair either.

spotdiff.win: Change only ONE thing, or results can’t be compared. Clue 1!

suredial.afterText: Try it: predict, say how sure you are, then test.
suredial.title: The how-sure dial

why.q: Why say how sure you are?
why.t: Scientists love the surprises. A prediction you were SURE about that turns out wrong teaches you the most.

todo: Pick a thing. Predict: will it stick?
Turn the dial: how sure are you?
Press Test it. A sure prediction that was wrong earns a gold star!

items.line: It stuck! A “tin” can is really steel with a very thin coat of tin.
Staples are thin steel wire. Snap!
No pull. The tray is aluminum.

suredial.goldLine: Big learning! You were sure, and you were wrong. Now you know something new.
suredial.q: Lots of scientists predict the “tin” can won’t stick, and they’re wrong. What does a wrong prediction mean?

opts.t: You found something new to learn. That’s how science works.

opts.miss: Look at the gold stars. A wrong prediction isn’t a failure. It’s a discovery.
The same magnet worked on the staple. Test results don’t lie.

suredial.win: Wrong predictions are gold. Names can fool you, so test! Clue 2!

notes2table.afterText: Help turn them into a real data table.
notes2table.title: Messy notes to a data table

why.t: They get lost, and they don’t say which thing they mean. A data table puts every result in its own row.

todo: Read a sticky note. Which thing is it about?
Drag it onto that row (or tap the note, then the row).
Fill all 8 rows. Watch the spoon!

rows.note: From the picnic basket. Has 4 points. SNAP! It stuck.
Also from the picnic basket. Shiny. “STAINLESS STEEL” stamped on it. Nothing?!
rows.miss: Which picnic thing is stamped “stainless steel”?

rows.note: Label says beans. Everybody calls it a tin can. It stuck!
rows.miss: Which thing has a beans label?

rows.note: From the tackle box. Heavy tool. Stuck hard.
rows.miss: Which heavy tool came from the tackle box?
Which thing is orange-brown and bendy?

rows.note: Number 14 from the duck race. Light and silver. Nothing.
rows.miss: Which thing has a race number on it?

rows.note: Off a root beer bottle. Crimped edges. Stuck!
rows.miss: Which thing came off a root beer bottle?

notes2table.emptyLine: Every note is in the table.

wowCard.t: Wow! The spoon is stainless STEEL, and it didn’t stick. Some stainless steel has so much nickel and chromium mixed in that a magnet hardly pulls it. Only a test can tell you, and only a table keeps the proof.

notes2table.q: Dana says, “It’s steel, so it goes in the steel bin.” Which row of the table proves her wrong?

opts.t: The spoon row: stainless steel, and no pull.

opts.miss: The fork stuck. That row agrees with Dana. Which steel thing did NOT stick?
Nobody thinks the duck is steel. Look for a “steel” thing that didn’t stick.

notes2table.win: The table caught it: not every steel sticks. Clue 3!

ruler.title: Slide to the jump

why.t: Slide something toward a strong magnet. If it’s magnetic, at some point it leaps across the gap. How far away that happens is its jump distance.

todo: Pick an item. Hold the slide button, or drag the item along the ruler toward the magnet.
Watch for a jump. Test all 8.
ruler.model: A model test with one strong magnet.

opts.t: The same magnet for every item

opts.why: A strong magnet and a weak one give different results. Then you can’t compare the materials.

opts.t: At the 10 cm mark, every time

opts.why: Start closer, and it jumps sooner. Same start, every time.

ruler.lockedLine: Fair test locked: the same magnet, and every item starts at the 10 cm mark.

items.line: Steel. It leaped across a 3 cm gap.
Plastic. It touched the magnet and just sat there.
Iron. It jumped from 4 cm away.
The stainless spoon again: no jump. The table agrees with Mo’s note.

ruler.dragTip: Or drag the item along the ruler toward the magnet.
ruler.noneWord: It touched the magnet. No pull at all.
ruler.q: Why did every item use the same magnet and start at the 10 cm mark?

opts.t: So the only thing that changed was the material. That’s a fair test.
To make the test go faster.
opts.miss: Speed isn’t the reason. Think about Kai and Mo: what went wrong when they changed things?
The nail jumped at 4 cm and the pin at 2 cm. Magnets work at many distances.

ruler.win: Same magnet, same start: only the material changed. Iron and steel jumped. Clue 4!

photos.title: A magnet as big as a table
todo: Tap each number on the photo.
Then match each job to its number.

why.t: A real photo from about 80 years ago, at a steel mill in Pennsylvania. A giant magnet on a crane lifts scrap steel so it can be melted into new steel.

photos.alt: A huge round magnet hangs from a chain under an overhead crane, above big piles of scrap metal in a steel mill yard. Blue sky and clouds behind.
photos.credit: Alfred T. Palmer, Office of War Information, Library of Congress (fsac.1a35061)

hotspots.label: The lifting magnet
hotspots.t: A giant electromagnet: a magnet that works only when electricity flows. Switch it on to grab steel, switch it off to drop it.

hotspots.label: The overhead crane
hotspots.t: The crane rolls along its rails to carry the magnet over the piles.

hotspots.label: The operator’s cab
hotspots.t: A worker sits in this little room and drives the crane and the magnet.

hotspots.label: Scrap steel
hotspots.t: Old steel waiting to be melted. The magnet picks up only the magnetic metal.

task.q: Match it: which number does each job?

items.step: Grabs steel when the power is on
items.evid: The electromagnet grabs steel when electricity flows.
items.miss: Look for the round thing on the chain.

items.step: Where a worker drives the crane
items.evid: The operator works from the cab.
items.miss: Look for the little room up high on the right.

items.step: Old steel waiting to become new steel
items.evid: Scrap steel gets melted and used again.

task.win: A recycling center sorts steel the same way you did: with a magnet. Just a much bigger one!

tool.name: Magnetic field viewer
tool.teaser: Put a steel plate, then an aluminum plate, in front of a magnet. Which one blocks the field?
tool.done: Tool of the Week: you found which plate blocks a magnetic field.

why.t: Scientists sprinkle iron filings, or use a special green film, to see a magnetic field that is invisible to our eyes.

fieldviewer.title: Block the field?
todo: Press Sprinkle and watch the filings.
Try all three, then answer the question.
fieldviewer.model: A model: each little line is a filing, turned the way the magnetic field points.

setups.note: The field spreads out on both sides of the magnet.
The steel plate soaks up the field. Behind it, the filings hardly line up at all.
The aluminum plate changes nothing. The field goes right through it.

q.q: Which plate blocked the magnet’s field?

opts.why: Steel is magnetic, so it pulls the field into itself. Aluminum isn’t magnetic, so the field passes right through.
Look again: behind the aluminum plate, the filings still line up.
Compare the two setups. Only one of them changed the filings.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell how to test fairly, or what counts as evidence?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A fair test changes only one thing, and a data table keeps every result as evidence.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “fair test”, “one thing” and “data table”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
